topic: JVM Internals (Memory Model, G1/ZGC, Class Loading)

questions.question: What is the primary architectural cause of this issue?
options: A) `@Async` requires a thread pool bean named `taskExecutor`; without it, Spring defaults to synchronous execution and suppresses `@Transactional`.

B) The internal self-invocation of `processOrder` bypasses the Spring CGLIB/JDK dynamic AOP proxy, executing the method in the caller's thread without proxy interception for `@Async` and `@Transactional`.
C) The JVM Memory Model does not guarantee visibility of `order.setStatus()` across worker threads without explicit synchronization.
D) `Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW` creates a deadlock with Spring's default thread pool when invoked in a tight loop.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) The internal self-invocation of `processOrder` bypasses the Spring CGLIB/JDK dynamic AOP proxy, executing the method in the caller's thread without proxy interception for `@Async` and `@Transactional`.
questions.explanation: Spring AOP leverages runtime proxies (either dynamic JDK proxies or CGLIB subclass proxies) to apply cross-cutting concerns like `@Transactional` and `@Async`. When `dispatchOrders()` invokes `processOrder()` using direct `this.processOrder()` method dispatch within the same class, the call target is the raw object instance (`this`), completely bypassing the surrounding proxy wrapper. Consequently, the method executes synchronously on the caller's thread within the existing transactional context (or lack thereof), ignoring both annotations.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where an analytics microservice running on OpenJDK 17 with ZGC (`-XX:+UseZGC`) crashes periodically with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`. Heap utilization remains stable under 35%, but Metaspace usage increases monotonically over several days. Heap dumps reveal millions of dynamically generated class metadata entries originating from a custom Groovy script evaluator that compiles expressions via custom `ClassLoader` instances.
questions.question: Why is the JVM unable to reclaim Metaspace memory during garbage collection cycles?
options: A) ZGC does not support concurrent class unloading; Metaspace can only be collected during a Full GC Stop-The-World pause.
B) Groovy compiled classes are placed in the Non-nmethods CodeCache segment, which is never reclaimed by GC.

C) A `ClassLoader` and all its loaded `Class` metadata in Metaspace can only be unloaded if the `ClassLoader` instance itself, all its defined classes, and all instances of those classes are strictly unreachable from any GC root.
D) Metaspace allocations are off-heap native memory buffers managed by `sun.misc.Unsafe` and cannot be tracked by garbage collection barriers.
questions.correct_answer_text: C) A `ClassLoader` and all its loaded `Class` metadata in Metaspace can only be unloaded if the `ClassLoader` instance itself, all its defined classes, and all instances of those classes are strictly unreachable from any GC root.
questions.explanation: In JVM internals, Metaspace memory allocation is tied to the lifecycle of the defining `java.lang.ClassLoader`. A dynamic class and its associated Metaspace metadata cannot be freed independently; the entire `ClassLoader` domain must be collected. If even a single static field, instance reference, or `ThreadLocal` retains a reference to a class or an instance of a class loaded by that `ClassLoader`, the `ClassLoader` remains reachable from the GC root set, entirely preventing Metaspace reclamation for all classes loaded by it.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a low-latency trading platform running on Java 21 with ZGC. While the average stop-the-world (STW) pauses are sub-millisecond (< 1ms), profiling reveals that during concurrent relocation phases, application mutator threads experience elevated CPU utilization and high tail-latency spikes (`p99.99`) when traversing deep object graphs across large in-memory caches.
questions.question: Which JVM internal mechanism in ZGC is directly responsible for this latency spike on application threads?
options: A) The write barrier executing store-store memory fences to preserve volatile variable semantics across CPU cores.
B) The load barrier intercepting dereferences of colored pointers pointing to relocated objects, forcing the application thread into a slow-path self-healing lookup and page update.
C) The Card Table dirtying mechanism triggering thread-local handshake stalls during generational card scanning.
D) The JIT compiler deoptimizing compiled bytecode back to interpreted mode during phase transition safepoints.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) The load barrier intercepting dereferences of colored pointers pointing to relocated objects, forcing the application thread into a slow-path self-healing lookup and page update.
questions.explanation: ZGC achieves sub-millisecond STW pauses by relocating objects concurrently while mutator threads are actively running. To guarantee correctness, ZGC uses 64-bit Colored Pointers (metadata bits stored directly in references) and JIT-compiled Load Barriers. When a thread loads a reference from the heap, the load barrier tests the pointer's color bits. If the reference points to an object in a relocation set that has moved or not yet been updated, the thread trips the load barrier's slow path: it resolves the new object location from the forwarding table, updates the reference ('self-healing'), and returns the updated pointer. Heavy memory graph traversal during concurrent relocation causes numerous slow-path executions on mutator threads, leading to CPU cache misses and tail-latency spikes.
